tldr: We propose HumanoidToolBench, a benchmark that integrally evaluates humanoids extending their physical limits—from functional tool selection to completing tasks by combining grasping, whole-body manipulation, and bipedal locomotion—along with ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k teleoperation demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real robot. The results reveal that even state-of-the-art robot foundation models exhibit a substantial gap between picking up a suitable tool and successfully using it to complete a task, with success rates dropping sharply once locomotion is introduced.
hero_caption: Overview of HumanoidToolBench. Built on the Unitree G1 humanoid platform, it comprises 18 tasks combining three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes. Using 55 tool assets and ToolBook—a dataset of 3,094 human demonstrations—it comprehensively evaluates seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot.
overview:
When humans face tasks beyond their reach or requiring high force, they solve them by selecting appropriate tools and skillfully coordinating their bodies. Humanoids operating in the real world similarly require tool use to overcome their inherent physical limits. However, existing benchmarks have been confined to tool grasping with stationary robot arms, tool understanding via visual question answering (VQA), or whole-body humanoid locomotion alone. A unified benchmark for evaluating the entire process—selecting a functionally suitable tool, grasping it, and completing a task while walking—was lacking.

To address this gap, this paper introduces HumanoidToolBench, a new benchmark comprehensively evaluating humanoids from tool selection to whole-body mobile manipulation. The tasks span three everyday scenarios: pushing a ball, retrieving a ball, and breaking ice. These are combined across three execution levels—tool pickup only (L0), stationary tool use (L1), and mobile tool use involving locomotion (L2)—and two tool-set modes, including a decoy mode containing functionally deficient distractors, yielding 18 tasks in total. The authors also present ToolBook, a dataset of 3,094 human teleoperation trajectories collected on the Unitree G1 in both simulation and the real world.

Evaluating seven policies in simulation (including GR00T N1.7) and three on the real robot showed that even when policies successfully recognize and lift the correct tool, their success rate drops substantially when attempting to apply the tool to the target and finish the task. In particular, success rates plummeted at L2 when locomotion was added. Detailed analyses also revealed lower selection accuracy on unseen tools and insensitivity to changing instruction texts, highlighting fundamental open challenges in tool use for current vision-language-action (VLA) models.
contributions: Built HumanoidToolBench, the first tool-use benchmark for humanoids that spans tool selection and pickup, stationary manipulation, and mobile manipulation with locomotion.
Released ToolBook, a large-scale dataset of 3,094 demonstrations collected via Meta Quest teleoperation in simulation and on the real Unitree G1.
Enabled decoupled failure analysis of tool selection versus execution by separating execution levels (L0/L1/L2) and decoy presence, combined with contact event tracking.

Quantified substantial gaps between tool grasping and task completion as well as the challenges of compound locomotion, through evaluations of seven simulation and three real-world policies alongside focused probe experiments.

sections.heading: Why humanoids need benchmarking from tool selection to mobile execution
sections.summary: Just as humans expand physical limits through tools, humanoids need tool use to work in human environments. However, existing benchmarks cover either tool selection or isolated manipulation, lacking a unified framework across selection, grasping, whole-body control, and walking. This paper fills the gap with the 18-task HumanoidToolBench and the 3.1k-demonstration ToolBook dataset.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to perform diverse tasks in human work environments, they must use tools to compensate for tasks beyond their physical reach or strength. Successful tool use requires selecting a tool with suitable functional properties, grasping it, and coordinating locomotion when needed to apply the tool's working end to the target object. How a tool is grasped alters its effective reach and the orientation of its working end (pushing, pulling, striking, etc.), and the robot must maintain geometric contact relationships with the target even while moving its body. A comprehensive evaluation across the entire process—from tool selection to task completion—is therefore essential.

Yet existing robotics benchmarks capture only fragments of this challenge. Benchmarks like HumanoidBench include spoon manipulation or window wiping, but do not assess the ability to select the right tool from multiple functional alternatives. Benchmarks specifically targeting tool use have either been limited to visual question answering (VQA) without physical embodiment, or restricted to stationary arm manipulators.

To bridge this divide, the authors developed HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark targeting the Unitree G1, alongside ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k human teleoperation demonstrations. To disentangle functional tool selection from execution success, the benchmark combines three scenarios (reach extension, retrieval, striking) across three execution levels (L0: pickup only, L1: stationary tool use, L2: mobile tool use) and two tool-set modes (standard, decoy). This design clearly exposes cases where a robot selects the right tool but fails execution, or gets deceived by visually similar decoys.

sections.heading: How it differs from existing humanoid and robot tool-use benchmarks
sections.summary: While manipulation and humanoid whole-body control benchmarks have advanced, none unite functional tool selection with mobile execution. Existing tool-use benchmarks also remain confined to stationary arms or VQA. This work is the first framework hierarchically integrating tool selection, whole-body manipulation, and bipedal locomotion.
sections.details:
The related work falls broadly into two categories: humanoid benchmarks and robotic tool-use benchmarks.

### Current state of humanoid benchmarks
Benchmarks such as LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 focus on single-arm or dual-arm manipulators and do not address whole-body control or locomotion challenges unique to humanoids. Recently, humanoid whole-body benchmarks like HumanoidBench, SIMPLE, and WOLF-VLA have emerged. However, while SIMPLE stages tasks, it involves no tool selection decisions, and WOLF-VLA does not release human demonstrations for training. In short, comprehensive evaluations that require selecting a functionally appropriate tool among multiple candidates and using it both statically and while walking have been absent.

### Current state of robot tool-use benchmarks
Tool use is a key cognitive ability that extends the body schema, yet its evaluation in robotics has remained limited. PhysToolBench assesses tool understanding in a VQA format without embodied actions; DexCraft focuses on single-arm grasping where the tool is already pre-grasped; and RoboWits examines dual-arm tool selection under unexpected situations without locomotion or whole-body control. Furthermore, none of these benchmarks stratify tasks by execution difficulty.

HumanoidToolBench evaluates the complete humanoid pipeline: choosing the right tool from 55 asset variations, grasping it, transporting it, and applying it to a target object. By combining execution levels that increase task difficulty with tool-set modes that increase selection difficulty, it uniquely enables detailed comparisons of a policy's functional understanding versus its physical control limits.

sections.heading: Task design and the full scope of the ToolBook dataset
sections.summary: Guided by real-world utility, interpretability, and functional selection, the authors designed 18 tasks (3 scenarios × 3 levels × 2 modes). Policies take Unitree G1 head camera images and proprioception as input and output locomotion and whole-body joint commands. ToolBook supports training and evaluation with 3,094 trajectories collected via Meta Quest teleoperation.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The robot receives a language instruction without explicit tool names (e.g., "pick up a tool and move the ball to the goal") and must select an appropriate tool from candidates in the scene to complete the task. The task is formulated as a goal-conditioned partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). The candidate set $\mathcal{B}$ includes a suitable tool $b^\star$, two irrelevant objects, and, in decoy mode, an unsuitable distractor tool. Observations $o_t = (I_t, \mathbf{x}_t)$ consist solely of head camera images $I_t$ and robot proprioceptive state $\mathbf{x}_t$ without ground-truth object states, requiring the policy to infer the appropriate tool directly from vision and language.

### III-B Design Principles and 18-Task Structure
The benchmark rests on three core principles:
- Real-world utility: Three everyday scenarios test functional tool roles—reach extension (BallMove: pushing a distant ball into a 0.12 m goal area with a long stick), retrieval (BallRetrieve: hooking and pulling a ball backward with a hooked stick), and force transmission (IceBreak: shattering two ice blocks using a hammer).
- Interpretability: Execution difficulty is graded across L0 (success upon picking up and lifting the tool by 0.08 m), L1 (tool use without locomotion), and L2 (locomotion to the opposite side of the table while holding the tool, followed by task execution). Contact events (candidate contact, target tool first contact, target tool lifted, tool-object contact, and final success) are tracked to pinpoint where failures occur.
- Functional selection: The standard mode (S) presents only one functional tool among distractors, whereas the decoy mode (D) introduces functionally flawed decoys such as sticks that are too short, straight sticks lacking hooks, or soft flyswatters and plungers.

### III-C Environment and Control Stack
Simulation is implemented in MuJoCo using the Unitree G1 (29 whole-body DoFs plus two 7-DoF Dex3 hands). Policy action outputs $a_t$ specify target joint angles for the hands, arms, and waist, alongside linear velocities $v_x, v_y$, yaw rate $\psi^\star$, and base height $z_t^\star$ for locomotion. Lower-body bipedal walking is governed by pre-trained GR00T Balance/Walk reinforcement learning controllers.

### III-D & III-E ToolBook Data Collection and Evaluation Protocol
Eight skilled operators gathered 1,200 successful L1/L2 simulation trajectories via Meta Quest VR teleoperation. An additional 1,803 L0 trajectories were derived by truncating these upon successful lift, and 91 demonstrations were collected on the physical G1, assembling ToolBook with 3,094 demonstrations in total. All 18 tasks are benchmarked in simulation, while real-robot evaluations test L1 BallMove and BallRetrieve across both standard and decoy modes.

captions.F2: Overall task structure of HumanoidToolBench. Across three scenarios (BallMove, BallRetrieve, IceBreak), three execution levels (L0: selection and pickup, L1: stationary use, L2: mobile use with locomotion) and two tool-set modes (standard, decoy) are crossed to form 18 tasks. Decoy mode introduces distractor tools that fail spatial length, affordance shape, or physical stiffness requirements.

sections.heading: Current limits and steep hurdles in tool use exposed by sim and real G1 tests
sections.summary: Evaluating seven policies in simulation and three on the physical G1 revealed that completing tasks (L1/L2) had significantly lower success rates than simply lifting the correct tool (L0). Adding locomotion in L2 drastically degraded performance, and policies proved fragile against decoy tools and unseen tool appearances.
sections.details:
### Main Experimental Findings and Performance Discrepancies
Simulation evaluations compared state-of-the-art baselines, including GR00T N1.7. Across all policies, a consistent and stark performance drop emerged between tool selection/pickup (L0) and actual task completion using the tool (L1/L2). Even policies achieving high accuracy at simply lifting a tool frequently failed when attempting to bring the tool's tip into precise contact with the ball or ice.

Furthermore, introducing walking in L2 caused success rates to plummet compared to L1. Coordinating stable tool holding with whole-body bipedal balancing, followed by precise re-approach to the target object after locomotion, remains a formidable barrier for current humanoid policies.

### Decoys and Diagnostic Probing Experiments
Introducing the decoy mode (D) lowered the rate of selecting and grasping the correct tool compared to the standard mode (S). Detailed contact event analysis revealed that low overall task success did not stem from failing to touch tools at all; rather, robots grasped the tool but could not manipulate the target properly, or mistakenly grabbed visually plausible decoy tools.

Focused probe experiments on GR00T N1.7 trained in standard mode uncovered two major vulnerabilities:
- Degraded representation on unseen valid tools: Presenting tools with novel shapes or textures unseen during training led to a marked drop in first-contact accuracy.
- Insensitivity to instruction variations: In a fixed IceBreak scene, the policy continued executing the striking motion even when fed completely unrelated instructions, showing an over-reliance on visual cues without genuine grounding in the functional semantics of language instructions.

Real-world Unitree G1 evaluations mirrored these findings: policies suffered from selection errors when decoys were present and failed from real-world contact uncertainties, validating both the efficacy of sim-to-real transfer with ToolBook and the steep challenges of real-world tool use.

takeaways: A massive performance gap exists between lifting a tool and completing a task with it, showing that grasping success alone cannot measure tool-use competence.
Adding humanoid bipedal locomotion (L2) drastically reduces task success, highlighting whole-body coordination between tool grasping and walking as a critical frontier.
Policies are fragile to decoy tools and unseen tool appearances, often acting on visual biases while ignoring language instructions, which calls for deeper functional affordance understanding.
limitations: Real-robot evaluations were restricted to stationary L1 BallMove and BallRetrieve due to safety and physical setup constraints, leaving mobile L2 tasks and high-impact IceBreak unverified on hardware.
Task scenarios were limited to pushing, pulling, and striking, leaving more complex, contact-rich tool manipulation such as twisting (screwdrivers) or cutting (scissors) unexplored.
